chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Sa'd ibn Abi Khalaf, who said:

I said to Abu Al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him): 'I had bought a slave girl secretly from my wife, and that reached her, so she went out from my house and refused to return to my house. So I went to her in the house of her family, and I said to her:
That which has reached you is false, and the one who brought this to you is your enemy, intending to cause separation between us.

She said: 'By Allah, there will never be goodness between me and you ever, until you swear to me by freeing every slave girl you own, and by giving your wealth in charity, if you have bought a slave girl and she is in your possession today.'
So I swore to her with that, and she made me repeat the oath and said to me: 'So say,
I said to her: 'Every slave girl of mine at this moment, so she is free.'
And I had separated from my slave girl and intended to free her and marry her for my desire regarding her.

He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is nothing upon you regarding what she made you swear, and know that neither freeing nor charity is valid except what is intended by it is the Face of Allah and His Reward.'
ai.seo_question: Does an oath to free slaves or give charity require the intention to be purely for Allah's sake to be valid?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the Shia juristic distinction between the validity of an oath (yamin) and the validity of the act sworn upon (ibadah), a key principle in Usul al-Fiqh. The Imam clarifies that while the oath remains binding even if the intention (niyyah) is merely to please the wife rather than for Allah's sake, the subsequent emancipation or charity only counts as a religiously valid act if performed with the specific intention of seeking Allah's reward. This highlights the nuance in Shia scholarship where the mechanical validity of a vow does not automatically confer spiritual merit to the associated action.
